utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Madam Registrar, would you please ask the accused to be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could the accused be seated and please could the headphones be given to him, so he can hear the President of the Trial Chamber. Can you hear me, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. You may be seated. We are now going to go on with the initial appearance, with the accused Goran Jelisic. Accused, would you please stand up, and please could you say your first and last name, your date and place of birth, your profession and the place where you lived when you were arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: My name is Goran Jelisic, I am also known by my nickname, Adolf. I was born on 7th June 1968 in Bijeljina and I am a mechanic for agricultural machinery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you tell me where your domicile was?

utterances.speaker: MR. JELISIC
utterances.text: Slobodana Jovanovic street, number 5, in Bijeljina in Republika Serbska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In Bijeljina. You may be seated, Mr Jelisic. I am going to ask you now what is the counsel -- who is the counsel who will defend you? Could you tell me who is your counsel or Defence? I would like to know who will appear on your behalf. Mr Jelisic, could you please confirm, I do not know whether you can hear the interpreters, could you please tell me who is your lawyer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JELISIC
utterances.text: Mr Igor Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The reason why I am asking is because the Registry informed me that there were some variations about that fact, I just wanted from you the confirmation that it was Mr Pantelic who was your counsel. Could you, Mr Pantelic, tell me that you are the chosen counsel, did you have a mandate given by Mr Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, this morning I arrange all necessary papers. I came yesterday to The Hague and furthermore, I would like also to inform this Trial Chamber that I will be acting in this case as lead counsel and my co-counsel is my distinguished colleague Mr Veselin Londrovic from Bijeljina and also I would like to inform you that I submitted all necessary papers including power of attorney, signed by Mr Jelisic, and stated that me and my colleague Mr Londrovic are his defence counsels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So Madam Registrar, could you please confirm what was just told by the accused on the one hand, who chose Mr Pantelic as his counsel and also I would like the confirmation that -- was it the accused who decided for two lawyers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Today we received in the Registry that Mr Pantelic should be the counsel, this was decided by the accused and when it comes to Mr Londrovic, it was decided some time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Jelisic, can I confirm then that you have two counsels, Mr Pantelic who is leading your defence, Mr Pantelic being the one who leads your defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is so. Mr Pantelic is your counsel for the Defence, with a colleague of his from Bijeljina whose name I have not understood, but Madam Registrar will be probably able to tell us the name.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is Mr Veselin Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would just like to tell you about the Rules, about our Statute and the procedure. According to Article 20 of our Statute, the indictment and the rights of the accused should be respected. I am going to speak later on in a bit more detail about those rights. We have to ensure that the accused has understood the contents of the indictment and ask him whether he pleads guilty or not guilty, and also there are certain rights of the accused, one of those being to be informed in a language that he understands and in details about the nature and the motives of the charges against him. The text of the Statute, voted in 1993 by the Security Council, have been completed by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, created by the judges from this Tribunal, and there are various Rules, out of those Rule 82, on which we are going to base ourselves today and so we have to proceed according to certain formalities. We have to read the indictment to the accused in a language that he speaks and understands and also we have to make sure that the accused understands the indictment. We have to hear whether he pleads guilty or not guilty on each count of the indictment, and then we have to see whether he pleads guilty or not guilty. In case the accused pleads not guilty, the Registrar has to decide about the date of the trial, and in case the accused pleads guilty to set the date for the verdict and also in case it is necessary, we have to fix all the other relevant dates. Now I am turning myself to Mr Pantelic. Is the indictment from July 1995, was it given -- was the indictment given to the accused, has the accused understood its contents?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that was done fully in accordance with the Rules of Procedure, but please allow me to give you some facts which might be very, very important before we move to today's session. The Defence would like to bring to your attention, your Honour, some very important facts. We are in possession of one very important document that might be related to this stage of procedure, in accordance with Rule 62. Unfortunately, due to the lack of time for preparation for this hearing, and due to the fact that I have received it immediately prior to this session today, I am giving all my apologies to this Trial Chamber for this inconvenience. The document in question might have substantial influence with regard to one of the fundamental principles of law, and that is fairness of trial, not to mention the other basic human rights, which are profoundly incorporated in the structure of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one very precise suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I have got a suggestion, but it is the President of the Trial Chamber who is to set the agenda for today. This is an initial appearance. Regardless of the fact what document it is, please do not interrupt me when it is not necessary. I am going to set the agenda for this trial, but please, I would like first of all to apply Article 62. I am going to turn myself now towards the Prosecution and I would like to have the appearances for the Prosecution, so could I please have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours, Terree Bowers and my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Vladimir Tochilovsky and we appear for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a second. I have a suggestion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But please could you take the floor only when I give you the floor. It is a question of politeness. Please would you respect the ontology of all legal institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need not public session for five minutes, not more, to submit to you a very important document and after that we can proceed. That is only my proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Maybe you need a private session, but I need a public session in order to confirm the indictment and this accused that has been arrested on the charges pressed against him according to the indictment from June 1995, and this needs to be done and then later on maybe I can grant your request and if necessary it can be done in private session, but before any other motions, because, you understand that, you are a very knowledgeable lawyer, but you do understand that we cannot do anything now before we start applying the procedure according to Article 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- In accordance with Rule 62. In that case, I request to have a closed session immediately after this hearing, if it is possible. That is my official request. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I will consult my colleagues. (Pause). The Chamber has decided that for the time being it will follow Rule 62 and we will have the indictment read, the indictment of 30th June 1995. After the reading, we will ask the accused to plead guilty or not guilty to each of the counts. If at that time the Defence has a request to make, that is in a closed session, it will be presented so that the Prosecutor can also express himself as well, but there is a fundamental principle which means that the initial -- at the initial appearance the indictment must be read to the accused. Madam Registrar, would you please start the reading of the indictment of 30th June 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor of the Tribunal against Goran Jelisic, also known as Adolf, and Ranko Cesic. Richard J Goldstone, Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, pursuant to his authority under Article 18 of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, charges: 1. Beginning on about 30th April 1992, Serb forces from Bosnia and elsewhere in the former Yugoslavia fought to obtain control of Brcko, a town and municipality in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the former Yugoslavia. Serb forces forcibly expelled Croat and Muslim residents from their homes and, with the assistance of local Serb authorities, held them at collection centres, where many were killed, beaten and otherwise mistreated. Many of the women, children and elderly were confined at the nearby village of Brezovo Polje. Most of the men of military age, and a few women, were taken to Luka camp. 2. From about 7th May 1992 until early July 1992, Serb forces confined hundreds of Muslim and Croat men, and a few women, at Luka camp in inhumane conditions and under armed guard. From about 7th May 1992 until about 21st May 1992, detainees were systematically killed at Luka. Almost every day during that time, the accused, often assisted by camp guards, entered Luka's main hangar where most detainees were kept, selected detainees for interrogation, beat them and then often shot and killed them. 3. The accused, often assisted by camp guards, usually shot detainees at close range in the head or back. Often, the accused and camp guards forced the detainees who were to be shot to put their heads on a metal grate that drained into the Sava River, so that there would be minimal clean-up after the shootings. The accused and guards then ordered other detainees to move the bodies to one of two disposal areas where the bodies were piled until they were later loaded on trucks and taken to mass graves outside the town of Brcko or disposed of in other ways. 4. From about 21st May 1992 until early July 1992, the detainees were subjected to beatings and, less frequently than before, killings. 5. In early July 1992, the surviving Luka detainees were transferred to another detention camp at Batkovic. 6. During the time Luka camp operated, the Serb authorities killed hundreds of Muslim and Croat detainees. The accused. 7. On about 1st May 1992, Goran Jelisic, who was born on 7th June 1968 in Bijeljina, came to Brcko from Bijeljina, where he had worked as an agricultural machinery mechanic. During most of May 1992, Goran Jelisic acted as the commander of Luka camp and called him the "Serb Adolf". 8. Ranko Cesic, who was born in 1964 in Drvar, lived in Brcko before the war. During May and June 1992, he acted under the apparent authority of the Brcko police and held a position of authority at Luka camp. General allegations. 9. Unless otherwise set forth below, all acts and omissions alleged in this indictment took place between about 17th April and 20th November 1992 in Brcko municipality in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. 10. At all times relevant to this indictment, a state of armed conflict and partial occupation existed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. 11. At all times relevant to this indictment, all persons described in this indictment as victims were protected by the Geneva Conventions of 1949. 12. At all relevant times, Goran Jelisic and Ranko Cesic were required to abide by the laws and customs governing the conduct of war, including the Geneva Conventions of 1949. 13. Goran Jelisic and Ranko Cesic are individually responsible for the crimes alleged against them in this indictment, pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Tribunal Statute. Individual criminal responsibility includes committing, planning, initiating, ordering or aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation or execution of any crime referred to in Articles 2 to 5 of the Tribunal Statute. 14. All acts and omissions charged as crimes against humanity were part of a widespread, systematic or large-scale attack directed against the Muslim and Croat civilian population of Brcko. 15. In each count of this indictment charging torture, the acts were committed by, or at the instigation of, or with the consent or acquiescence of, an official or person acting in an official capacity, and for one or more of the following purposes: to obtain information or a confession from the victim or a third person; to punish the victim for an act the victim or a third person committed or was suspected of having committed; to intimidate or coerce the victim or a third person; and/or for any reason based upon discrimination of any kind. 16. Paragraphs 9 to 15 are re-alleged and incorporated into each of the charges set forth below. Charges: count 1, genocide. 17. In May 1992, Goran Jelisic, intending to destroy a substantial or significant part of the Bosnian Muslim people as a national, ethnical or religious group, systematically killed Muslim detainees at the Laser Bus company, the Brcko police station and Luka camp. He introduced himself as the "Serb Adolf", said that he had to come to Brcko to kill Muslims and often informed the Muslim detainees and others of the number of Muslims he had killed. In addition to killing countless detainees, whose identities are unknown, Goran Jelisic ordered or personally killed the victims described in paragraphs 18, 20-30, 35 and 38. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered, committed or aided and abetted: Count 1: genocide, a crime recognised by Article 4(2)(a) of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. JELISIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Jelisic, please allow the indictment to be read in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Counts 2-4, killing of Kemal Sulejmanovic. 18. On about 5th or 6th May 1992, Goran Jelisic, accompanied by several soldiers, entered the Laser Bus company building in Brcko and announced to the detainees that he was the "Serb Adolf". Goran Jelisic took the Muslim detainee Kemal Sulejmanovic, also known as Kemo, from the building and shot and killed him. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered or committed: Count 2: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 3, a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 4, a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 5-7, killing of Sakib Becirevic and four other men. 19. On about 5th May 1992, Ranko Cesic went to the Brcko Partizan Sports Hall where Muslim civilian were being confined, and took the Muslim detainee Sakib Becirevic, also known as Kibe, and four other men, named "Pepa", "Sale" and the two sons of a man called Avdo outside the hall. Ranko Cesic lined up and shot and killed the five detainees with bursts of gunfire. By these actions, Ranko Cesic committed: Count 5: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 6: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 7: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 8-10, killing of unknown male. 20. On about 6th or 7th May 1992, Goran Jelisic escorted an unknown male detainee down a street near the Brcko police station and then shot him in the head with a Scorpion pistol. By these actions, Goran Jelisic committed: Count 8: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 9: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 10: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Count 11-13, killing of Hasan Jasarevic. 21. On about 7th May 1992, Goran Jelisic, using a Scorpion pistol, shot and killed Hasan Jasarevic, a Muslim detainee who had fled the Brcko police station. By these actions, Goran Jelisic committed: Count 11. A grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 12: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 13: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 14-16, killing of a young man from Sinteraj. 22. On about 7th May 1992, Goran Jelisic left the Brcko police station with a young man from the neighbourhood of Sinteraj, whose identity is unknown. Goran Jelisic escorted the young man away from the police station to an area where the young man was shot and killed. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered or committed: Count 14: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 15: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 16: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal. Counts 17-19, killing of Ahmet Hodzic or Hadzic. 23. On about 7th May 1992, Goran Jelisic took the Muslim detainee Ahmet Hodzic, also known as Papa, a leader of the Brcko SDA (Muslim political party) outside the Brcko police station and beat him with a baton. Together with two guards, Goran Jelisic took Ahmet Hodzic to the same place where Goran Jelisic, earlier that day, had killed a young detainee from Sinteraj. Goran Jelisic told Ahmet Hodzic that he was looking at his town for the last time and then killed him. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered, committed or aided and abetted: Count 17: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 18: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 19: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 20-22, killing of Suad. 24. On about 7th May 1992, Goran Jelisic took a Muslim detainee named Suad from the Brcko police station and beat him with a rifle butt. Goran Jelisic, together with some soldiers, walked Suad to the same area where Goran Jelisic, earlier that day, had killed Ahmet Hodzic and a young man from Sinteraj. After reaching the area, Suad was shot and killed. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered, committed or aided and abetted: Count 20: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 21: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 22. A crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 23-25, killing of Amir Novalic. 25. On about 7th May 1992, Goran Jelisic shot and killed the Muslim detainee Amir Novalic, also known as Fric, inside the Brcko police station. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered or committed: Count 23: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 24: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 and of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 25, a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 26-28, killing of Sead Cerimagic and Jasminko Cumurovic. 26. On about 8th May 1992, Goran Jelisic and Ranko Cesic took the Muslim detainee Sead Cerimagic (also known as Cita) and Jasminko Cumurovic (also known as Jasce and Jasmin) from the main hangar building at Luka camp and shot and killed them. By these actions, Goran Jelisic and Ranko Cesic instigated, ordered, committed or aided and abetted: Count 26: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 27: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 28: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 29-31, killing of Huso and Smajil Zahirovic. 27. On about 8th May 1992, at Luka camp, Goran Jelisic accused two Muslim brothers from Zvornik, Huso and Smajil Zahirovic, of fighting for the Muslim resistance. Goran Jelisic took them outside of the main hangar building where they were shot and killed. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered or committed: Count 29: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 30: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions;. Count 31: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 32-37, torture and killing of Naza Bukvic. 28. On about 9th May 1992, near the main hangar building at Luka camp, Goran Jelisic, Ranko Cesic and others questioned the Muslim detainee Naza Bukvic about the whereabouts and activities of her brother, beat her with police batons and a shovel and then killed her. By these actions, Goran Jelisic and Ranko Cesic instigated, ordered, committed or aided and abetted: Counts 32-33: grave breaches recognised by Articles 2(b) (torture) and 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Counts 34-35: violations of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (torture) and (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Counts 36-37: crimes against humanity recognised by Articles 5(f) (torture) and 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 38-40, killing of Muharem Ahmetovic. 29. On about 9th May 1992, Goran Jelisic called the Muslim detainee Muharem Ahmetovic, the father of Naza Bukvic, from the main hangar building at Luka camp and killed him. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered or committed: Count 38. A grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 39: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 40, a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 41-43, killing of Stipo Glavocevic. 30. On about 9th May 1992, Goran Jelisic brought a Croat detainee named Stipo Glavocevic (also known as Stjepo), who had at least one ear cut off and was covered in blood, into the main hangar building at Luka and forced him to kneel in the centre of the hangar. Goran Jelisic beat Stipo Glavocevic. Goran Jelisic then directed a guard to shoot and kill Stipo Glavocevic just outside the entrance to the main hangar. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered, committed or aided and abetted: Count 41: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 42: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 43: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 44-46, killing of Sejdo. 31. On about 9th May 1992, Sejdo, a Muslim fisherman whose last name is unknown, arrived at Luka camp in the trunk of a car. Ranko Cesic put Sejdo in a small warehouse, beat him and then shot and killed him. By these actions, Ranko Cesic committed: Count 44. A grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 45: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 46: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 47-49, killing of Mirsad Glavovic. 32. On about 11th May 1992, Ranko Cesic called the Muslim policeman Mirsad Glavovic from the main hangar building at Luka camp. Ranko Cesic ordered Mirsad Glavovic to say goodbye and shake hands with the other detainees. Ranko Cesic then took Mirsad Glavovic outside the hangar building, beat him and killed him. By these actions, Ranko Cesic instigated, ordered or committed: Count 47: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 48: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 49: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 50-52, sexual assault. 33. On about 11th May 1992, at Luka camp, Ranko Cesic forced, at gun point, Muslim detainees A and B, who were brothers detained there, to beat each other and perform sexual acts on each other in the presence of others, causing them great humiliation and degradation. By these actions, Ranko Cesic instigated, ordered or committed: Count 50: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(b) (inhuman treatment) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 51: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(c) (humiliating and degrading treatment) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 52: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(g) (rape, which includes other forms of sexual assault) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 53-55, beatings of Zejcir and Resad Osmic. 34: between 10th and 12th May 1992, Goran Jelisic participated in the interrogation and beating of the Muslim brothers Zejcir and Resad Osmic. Goran Jelisic beat Zejcir and Resad Osmic with a baton and cut Resad Osmic's forearms with a military knife. Both brothers suffered head injuries, and Resad lost consciousness as a result of the beatings. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered or committed: Count 53: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(c) (wilfully causing great suffering) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 54: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (cruel treatment) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 55: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(i) (inhumane acts) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 56-58, killing of Novalija. 35. On about 12th May 1992, in the main hangar building at Luka camp, Goran Jelisic beat Novalija, an elderly Muslim man, with a metal pipe, shovel and wooden stick. Novalija died as a result of the beatings. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered or committed: Count 5 6: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 57: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 58: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 59-61, killing of Nihad Jasarevic. 36. On about 12th or 13th May 1992, in the main hangar building at Luka camp, Ranko Cesic and another person beat the Muslim detainee Nihad Jasarevic with a wooden club that contained a lead cylinder, killing Nihad Jasarevic. By these actions, Ranko Cesic instigated, ordered, committed or aided and abetted: Count 59: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 60: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 61: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 62-64, beatings of Muhamed Bukvic. 37. On about 13th May 1992, at Luka, Goran Jelisic used a baton to beat the Muslim detainee Muhamed Bukvic over his entire body. By these actions, Goran Jelisic committed: Count 62: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(c) (wilfully causing great suffering) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 63: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (cruel treatment) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 64: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(i) (inhumane acts) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 65-67, killing of Adnan Kucalovic. 38. On about 18th May 1992, Goran Jelisic called the Muslim detainee Adnan Kucalovic from the main hangar at Luka. Goran Jelisic accused Adnan Kucalovic of having a brother who was fighting with the Muslim resistance. Goran Jelisic then participated in the shooting and killing of Adnan Kucalovic. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered, committed or aided and abetted: Count 65: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 66: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 67: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 68-70, beatings of Amir Didic. 39. Between about 20th May and 28th May 1992, Goran Jelisic interrogated and regularly beat the Muslim detainee Amir Didic with a baton, a cable and nozzle of a fire hose, causing Amir Didic to lose consciousness. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered or committed: Count 68: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(c) (wilfully causing great suffering) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 69: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (cruel treatment) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 70: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(i) (inhumane acts) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 71-73, killing of two unknown males. 40. Between about 1st June and 6th June 1992, Ranko Cesic took four detainees, whose identities are unknown, from the office building at Luka camp to the paved road in front of the main hangar building and, with the assistance of two guards, shot and killed at least two of the detainees. By these actions, Ranko Cesic instigated, ordered, committed or aided and abetted: Count 71: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (wilful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 72: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 73: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 74-76, general conditions at Luka camp. 41. From about 7th May to about 28th May 1992, Goran Jelisic, acting as the commander of Luka, created an atmosphere of terror by killing, abusing and threatening the detainees, thereby subjecting them to extreme psychological trauma, degradation and fear of bodily injury and death. Goran Jelisic also created and maintained inhumane conditions at Luka by depriving them of adequate food, water, medical care and sleeping and toilet facilities. Ranko Cesic assisted Goran Jelisic in creating the atmosphere of terror and the inhumane conditions at Luka. By these actions, Goran Jelisic and Ranko Cesic instigated, ordered, committed or aided and abetted: Count 74: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(c) (wilfully causing great suffering) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 75: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (cruel treatment) of the Geneva Conventions;. Count 76: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(i) (inhumane acts) of the Tribunal Statute. Count 77, plunder of private property. 42. From about 7th May to about 28th May 1992, Goran Jelisic participated in the plunder of money, watches and other valuable property belonging to persons detained at Luka camp, including Hasib Begic, Zejcir Osmic, Enes Zukic and Armin Drapic. By these actions, Goran Jelisic instigated, ordered, committed or aided and abetted: Count 77. A violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3(e) (plunder) of the Tribunal Statute. Signed Richard J Goldstone, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Goran Jelisic, you may be seated. The Tribunal has taken note of the fact that you have pleaded not guilty to all of the counts contained in the indictment produced by the Prosecutor. Having said this, which is now the reality of this case file, I turn to the Prosecutor to ask where we are with the proceedings. Mr Prosecutor, are you now prepared to set the date for a hearing, and then I have to ask Mr Pantelic if he would like to file any preliminary motions. I have not forgotten the request that Mr Pantelic wanted to make. Mr Prosecutor, are you prepared, subject to any delays that would be caused by preliminary motions from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are prepared to move forward at the court's pleasure. We would need approximately two months to relocate witnesses but this case is essentially in a trial-ready format and we are ready to proceed as soon as the court has a courtroom available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment. I would not like to mix up technical and legal problems. My question was that if Mr Pantelic does not ask for his right of a 60 day delay to file preliminary motions, would you be ready to proceed to trial, regardless of the technical problems concerning the room? You said that you would need two months to call the witnesses. What do you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we could start as soon as the court pleases, but we need to just relocate some of the witnesses in the various areas of the former Yugoslavia and Europe, but when we submitted this indictment it was in a trial-ready format, it is simply primarily the logistics of relocating these people. Many of these individuals were at refugee camps, areas such as that, so they probably have relocated since the filing of the indictment, but we are prepared to proceed as soon as the court would like us to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has taken note that a trial could start relatively soon. Before I give the floor to Mr Pantelic, I would like to remind you that you have to give all the exhibits, all the material that was given with the indictment to one of the judges of this Tribunal, who is not in this Trial Chamber, together with all the witness statements. Can you give all these documents and within what delay?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, all of those documents have been provided to the accused before this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is true, we have -- I will show you, it is not more than 50 pages of supporting material, which is I assume at this moment everything which the Prosecutor has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There is nothing else, you only have the 50 pages, is that all?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, those are the confirming materials that we submitted to the confirming judge in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You may be seated. Mr Prosecutor, about how many witnesses do you plan to call in during the -- in the trial of Goran Jelisic, about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we think we would have a total of between 30 and 40 witnesses. We intend to dispense with the Article 2 charges so that we would not be putting on the general evidence with regard to international conflict, that should significantly expedite the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are asking for a modification, an amendment to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, not at this time. We will submit a formal motion to the court for withdrawal of the Article 2 charges. I just mention this to the court so that it can take that into account in judging the length of the trial. In cases involving Article 2 charges, it is necessary to present general evidence of the international conflict. If we withdraw the Article 2 charges then we will not have to present that type of evidence before the court and it should significantly shorten the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Prosecutor, I would like you to confirm that for the time being you have no other materials to disclose to the Defence. We do agree on that, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you very much. I now turn to Mr Pantelic. You confirm that you received all of the documents which accompanied the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: From this point on, on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to know whether, in principle, you do not have to answer immediately, whether you intend to take advantage of the 60 days that are available to you, that is 60 days which would take us to 26th May, in order to file preliminary motions. Let me remind you, although you must be familiar with our procedures, you know that Rule 62 says that after the initial hearing, one of the parties may raise one or several preliminary motions. Do you intend to do so or do you prefer to reflect on that? Are you sure that you are not going to file preliminary motions? This is important for the drafting of the provisional calendar for the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to the quantity and quality of material that is submitted to the Defence prior to this hearing, the Defence is ready for tomorrow to set up trial. We are absolutely ready for tomorrow, so it is up to this Trial Chamber to arrange that. It is really not so serious after all these years of collecting the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This means, Mr Pantelic, I want this to be in the record, that you are not going to file any preliminary motions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I can say we shall not make any pre-trial motions at this moment, but if suddenly some exceptional circumstances will arise, well, I will reconsider my position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We then remind you that you have 60 days for filing these preliminary motions, or else we will wait for the 60 days to pass in order to set the trial, or else at a given point you will simply state that you are waiving your right to go through to the end of the 60 days. At this point, we are not asking you to commit yourself definitively because, if I have understood you correctly, you are stating you are not going to lodge any preliminary motions but that possibly in the future there might be some and that you wish to reflect further on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, but as I stressed I would like on behalf of my client and in the name of the Defence, if it is possible, to hear the right date for the trial, so we can set a trial date now. The Defence is absolutely ready for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Prosecutor, would you like to propose a date? Does Madam Registrar have a date that she can suggest, or more specifically and completely speaking for any kind of technical implications that might arise out of this, would you prefer to think about it for a while or to speak about it with the Prosecutor. Do you have an idea as to the date of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, I think if we had 60 days to confirm the locations of our witnesses and to go out and recontact them that that would probably be sufficient time for us to actually get all of the witnesses arranged to begin their trial testimony, so it would just require essentially a two month period for resolving some of the logistical problems of locating the witnesses, making arrangements for them to come to The Hague et cetera. Our investigation is complete, we do not anticipate any additional investigation, it is just going back and confirming with people we have already interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will not set the date today, but we note that the Prosecutor needs a maximum of two months, I say a maximum of two months, in order to relocate the 30 to 40 witnesses, and Mr Pantelic, about how many witnesses do you intend to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Roughly saying, I think around 50, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, your Honour, excluding expert witnesses, of course, of which I have not more than five or six, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So you would have at least 50 and about 40 -- I am trying to look at the largest figures. Therefore there would be about 90 witnesses, which means that like the others, these trials will be rather long and then it would be best to start as quickly as possible. Therefore although we cannot control everything, we can say that starting today the time period -- the 60 day period for filing the preliminary motions will start to be counted, even though some may not be used, and that the Prosecutor needs about 60 days in order to find the witnesses so in any case, the date cannot be set before the end of March or the beginning of April. I therefore suggest that we set a date for a status conference which we could hold at about the end of February, that is halfway through the 60 days, by which time Mr Pantelic will have a better idea whether, with the agreement of his client, he plans to file preliminary motions or perhaps he wants to wait for any possible amendments that may be made by the Prosecutor to the indictment and at that point, we will have a better idea about how much time the Prosecutor will need in order to find the witnesses. Therefore I suggest Mr Fourmy, who is the legal officer of the Trial Chamber, I do not know if we can set the date for the status conference because we have to see whether the courtroom is available, but it will be a closed hearing which will probably take place around the end of February, perhaps 27th or 28th? We would need about one hour, maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: That would be possible around the end of February. I would like to recall that there has been a recent schedule change which gives us three possible days, 18th, 19th and 20th February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What about the last week? For 23rd, 24th, 25th and 26th February, but if we were to do that, that would correspond with the time of the Blaskic hearings and there would be the double sessions, the Aleksovski and Blaskic hearings for that second time of the month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The last date of the last week we might hold our status conference at 9.00 or 2.00, subject to the availability of Mr Pantelic. We will inform you of the specific date, but at least we have agreed that we would meet at the mid point of the 60 days, that is the time for filing the preliminary motions and the time you need in order to locate your witnesses. I think a month from now we will see things a bit more clearly. At that point, we will see where we are as regards disclosure of documents to Mr Pantelic. It seems for one time all the documents have been disclosed, which is not the case in all the trials. I can only congratulate you for that. At that point, complete with the other Trial Chambers and other benches of judges, we will be able to set the date for trial as quickly as possible. If the Prosecutor has nothing else to say, Mr Pantelic wishes to file a motion in closed session. Do you still wish to plead your motion in a closed session or is that no longer necessary? Do you want to speak about it in public? As you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As I stressed, your Honour, it was not in whole form an official motion, it was just a simple document, but in this particular case, I can proceed with this explanation in closed session, if you find that it is important; if not, in further period I will inform you by our official ways, according to the Rules, of course. So the question is only about one document, nothing more, without some big speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr Prosecutor, perhaps the document could be submitted and then we can evaluate it. What is your opinion, Mr Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are at a loss at this point, we are not sure what the document is, but we are certainly willing to discuss it with the Defence and resolve any difficulties with the particular document. It is conceivable that this could be resolved outside of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you do not need the judges, that is perfect. Mr Pantelic, perhaps you could come to an agreement with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is not so directed to the Prosecutor. Mostly it is for the knowledge of this Trial Chamber, so I do not see any particular reason to have any additional conference with the Prosecutor. It was only, as I stressed, for the judicial record and for the use of this Trial Chamber. That is simple. I cannot do that in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I wish to consult with my colleagues. (Pause). The Trial Chamber has decided that the initial appearance hearing is now complete and we can speak with the lawyer about the document that he wishes to produce. At this point, we will go into a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will go back into public session, have the accused brought in, after which we will terminate the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Mr President, I have just one matter of clarification regarding the discovery that we have provided to the accused, if we could just address that briefly when the accused returns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. The accused is coming back. Have him brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Jelisic, you may be seated. Mr Jelisic, your counsel has presented the problem which concerned him to us, and we thought it would be good to speak with you. Before we give you the floor one final time, Mr Prosecutor, you had a question you wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr President, just as a matter of clarification I wanted to make it clear that the materials we have provided to the Defence is all of the confirmation materials in its entirety, no redactions, but with regard to the witness statements and the documentary evidence for trial, we have not provided that as of yet, but we can do that very expeditiously if an expedited trial date is set. I just wanted to put this clarification on the record so there is no misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that was a good thing that you did. I was very pleasantly surprised that you had disclosed everything already -- in fact I was a little bit surprised. So we have agreed, I was saying a trial with only 50 pages, that is really quite exceptional, but I commit you then in accordance with Rule 62(A) that any declarations or other statements you have will be discussed during the status conference at the end of the hearing. The closed hearing is now complete and the judges would very much wish to hear what Mr Goran Jelisic has to say. Have you any comments you would like to make, Mr Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JELISIC
utterances.text: I have nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case, court stands adjourned.
